q8.answer: They are kept server-side in Redis under key gauth:{state} (code_verifier, nonce, origin, next, and user_id for settings), with a 600 s TTL. The browser also gets an HttpOnly gstate cookie holding the state value. The callback removes the Redis record with GETDEL as its first Redis step and clears the gstate cookie. If the callback never comes, the TTL expires the record.

q9.answer: It is held in Redis under glink:{ticket}, which stores google_sub, the matched user_id and next, with a 600 s TTL that wrong passwords do not extend. The browser refers to it through an HttpOnly gticket cookie holding the ticket id. It is deleted on successful link, on account lockout (including when the form is submitted while already locked), or when the final re-check refuses. Otherwise the TTL expires it.

q10.answer: It is stored in a new PostgreSQL table, user_google_accounts(user_id, google_sub, linked_at). user_id is the PRIMARY KEY, so a user has at most one Google account. google_sub is UNIQUE, so a Google account links to at most one user. The code checks first for clear messages, and a unique violation from a race is treated as refused.

q11.answer: The user is redirected back to the origin page (login keeps next) with a neutral message, "We could not complete Google sign-in. Try again or use email and password." Nothing is changed. A bad ID token (signature, iss, aud, exp or nonce) gets the same treatment. There is no retry. The authorization code is single-use and the state is already consumed, so the user starts over.

q12.answer: The origin field stored in the gauth record tells the callback which path to take, login or settings. For settings, the record also stores the user_id taken from the sid session when the flow started. At the callback, if the current sid user differs from that stored user_id, it shows the error page. The link is attached to that stored, verified user, and no session is started.
